• Approximately 335 people are receiving training in social urban planning and public management, thanks to the partnership between the Medellín Mayor's Office and EAFIT University.

• The Urban Studies Program: Medellín Transforming a City, aims to develop critical citizens who can address social and urban challenges.

With master classes, workshops, and educational tours through different parts of the city—areas where social transformation has taken center stage through urban interventions such as the Library Parks, the Integrated Transportation System, and the escalators in Comuna 13—groups of citizens are participating in the Urban Chair: Medellín, Transforming a City, offered by EAFIT University through its Center for Urban and Environmental Studies (Urbam), the Center for Political Analysis, and the Summer School.

Since last May, approximately 335 people from various fields have been selected through a public call for applications to receive this civic training, thanks to the Lee Kuan Yew Social Urbanism Award, considered the Nobel Prize for cities, which was awarded to Medellín by the government of Singapore in 2016. The Medellín Mayor's Office allocated the resources from this international prize, close to 600 million pesos, to fund the academic program for Medellín residents.

“This course has a very comprehensive approach, focusing on the city as a whole. It considers not only urban planning, in terms of urban or architectural design, but also public management. This is important because it provides a large group of people with analytical tools that will help them identify the challenges facing Latin American cities in general as they navigate these complex times,” says Valentina Franco Manchola, political scientist and academic coordinator of the course.

This international award, presented to 110 representatives from cities around the world, recognizes Medellín for its transformation from one of the most violent cities in Latin America to one of the most innovative. These characteristics, along with the city's historical transformation over the last 30 years, are the themes highlighted by the course.

“When dealing with urban issues, it’s important for people to have their own perspective on the territory. To that end, we conduct tours of sites throughout the city where participants can identify interesting dynamics in public spaces, where significant interventions have taken place that have marked a turning point, and where community work is underway,” explains Valentina, who holds a master’s degree in urban and environmental processes.

The academic program, coordinated by experts from Urbam and the Center for Political Analysis, lasts 40 hours and will run until the end of 2017 with various selected groups of citizens. As part of the course, the participants receive theoretical training in topics related to urban planning, public administration, security, and citizen participation.

“This urban and social transformation doesn't happen in a vacuum, but rather within the framework of public management, through the introduction of elements of collaborative governance, corporate citizenship, and public-private partnerships, all of which have been crucial in triggering the processes of change the city has undergone,” states Laura Gallego Moscoso, coordinator of the Center for Political Analysis.

Experts explain that the benchmarks for urban and social transformation in Medellín have arisen from the collaboration between different public and private sectors, the contributions of academia, and the work of the communities themselves in their territories. Together, these efforts have contributed to the impact of various social urbanism projects on the city.

“Medellín has the task of reflecting on itself, of challenging itself because it is a city that still has many problems to solve. And this is one of the most interesting objectives of the program: to bring together a group of citizens to reflect on the city's challenges and difficulties, forming a critical, conscious, and organized citizenry capable of mobilizing change,” says Valentina Franco.

In this course, rather than highlighting Medellín's achievements in urban and civic transformation, the aim is to identify the challenges urban environments face in achieving greater inclusion and equity. It is a commitment to the future.

“Urban and social transformation cannot be analyzed without understanding the processes of transformation in the public sphere, of more open governments. Medellín's transformation process has been two-pronged: one from the top down, where leaders connected to the public sphere have made strategic decisions that have generated change, but also projects that have emerged from social, community, and artistic spheres, which have leveraged processes of change in the city,” notes Laura Gallego.
